questions.q_en: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic feature of the Plant Kingdom?
options_en: Presence of a cell wall made of chitin
questions.solution_en:
• Plants have cell walls made of cellulose, not chitin. Chitin is characteristic of fungi, not plants. Other options reflect true characteristics of plants:

• Autotrophic nutrition

○ Plants produce their own food through photosynthesis.

• Eukaryotic cell structure

○ Plant cells are eukaryotic, containing a defined nucleus.

• Chlorophyll presence

○ Chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis in plants.

Further Insight:

• Characteristic Features of the Plant Kingdom:

○ Plants are eukaryotic and multicellular organism.

○ Plant cells have rigid cell walls composed primarily of cellulose, providing structural support.

○ Plants are autotrophic, meaning they produce their own food through photosynthesis, using sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water.

○ Plants contain chloroplasts, specialized organelles that carry out photosynthesis, where the light energy is converted into chemical energy.

○ Plants exhibit an alternation of generations in their life cycle, alternating between a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte stage.

○ Reproduction can be sexual (involving gametes) or asexual (vegetative propagation).

■ In higher plants, reproduction involves the formation of seeds, while lower plants reproduce through spores.

○ Plants are non-motile and remain fixed in one place due to their roots anchoring them in the ground.

○ Higher plants (like pteridophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms) possess vascular tissues like xylem and phloem for the conduction of water, nutrients, and food.

○ Plants store food, usually in the form of starch or other carbohydrates, for later use.

questions.q_en: Which class of algae is characterized by the presence of chlorophyll a and chlorophyll d, and is predominantly marine?
questions.solution_en:
• Rhodophyceae (red algae) are mainly marine and contain chlorophyll a and chlorophyll d.

• Chlorophyceae (Green algae): Contains chlorophyll a and b, found in freshwater.

• Phaeophyceae (Brown algae): Contains chlorophyll a and c, mostly marine.

• Cyanophyceae: Also known as blue-green algae, contains chlorophyll a.

Further Insight:

• Algae

• Chlorophyll-bearing, autotrophic, and aquatic organisms (found in freshwater and marine habitats).

• Reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation and sexually by the formation of gametes.

• Classes of Algae:

○ Chlorophyceae (Green Algae): Freshwater, chlorophyll a & b, e.g., Chlamydomonas, Ulothrix.

○ Phaeophyceae (Brown Algae): Marine, chlorophyll a & c, e.g., Fucus, Sargassum.

○ Rhodophyceae (Red Algae): Marine, chlorophyll a & d, e.g., Polysiphonia, Gelidium.

• Used in food (e.g., Laminaria, Sargassum).

• Source of iodine and antibiotic properties.

questions.q_en: Which of the following structures help Bryophytes in reproduction through water?
questions.solution_en:
• Bryophytes have antheridia (male) and archegonia (female) reproductive structures, which require water for the movement of sperm. Other options:

• Bryophytes lack vascular tissues.

• Sporangia: Present in Pteridophytes and other plants for spore production.

• Phloem: Absent in Bryophytes; they lack true vascular systems.

Further Insight:

• Bryophyta

• Known as the amphibians of the plant kingdom, dependent on water for reproduction.

• Non-vascular plants found in moist, shaded habitats.

• Examples: Liverworts (e.g., Marchantia), Mosses (e.g., Funaria), Hornworts.

• Plant body has root-like, stem-like, and leaf-like structures.

• Reproduction involves antheridia (male) and archegonia (female), producing spores and gametophytes.

questions.q_en: Which of the following distinguishes Pteridophytes from Bryophytes?
options_en: Lack of roots, stems, and leaves
questions.solution_en:
• Pteridophytes are the first plants to have vascular tissues (xylem and phloem). Other options:

• Both groups have independent gametophytes.

• Both groups reproduce using spores.

• Pteridophytes have well-differentiated roots, stems, and leaves, unlike Bryophytes.

Further Insight:

• Pteridophyta

• First terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues (xylem and phloem).

• Well-differentiated plant body with roots, stems, and leaves.

• Reproduce through spores produced in sporangia.

• Examples: Ferns, Horse-tails, Marsilea.

questions.q_en: Which division of plant bears naked seeds?
questions.solution_en:
• Gymnosperms bear naked seeds, which are not enclosed within fruits, unlike angiosperms.

• Angiosperms: Seeds enclosed within fruits.

• Bryophytes: Reproduce via spores, not seeds.

• Pteridophytes: Also reproduce by spores, not seeds.

Further Insight:

• Gymnosperms

• Non-flowering, seed-bearing plants with seeds that are exposed (not enclosed in fruits).

• Examples: Pinus, Cycas, Cedrus.

• Features:

○ Woody, perennial, and may form large trees.

○ Taproot system, with leaves that may be simple or compound.

○ Reproduce through heterospory (microspores and megaspores).

•

questions.q_en: Which of the following is NOT true for Angiosperms?
questions.solution_en:
• Angiosperms have well-developed vascular tissues (xylem and phloem).

• Presence of flowers: A distinguishing feature of angiosperms.

• Double fertilization: A unique reproductive feature in angiosperms.

• Seeds enclosed in fruits: One of the key characteristics of angiosperms.

Further Insight:

• Angiosperms

• Flowering plants with seeds enclosed in fruits.

• Exhibit great diversity in size

○ Smallest angiosperm: Wolffia

○ Largest angiosperm: Eucalyptus

• Pollen grains and ovules are developed in specialized structures called flowers.

• Angiosperms are divided into:

○ Monocotyledons

○ Dicotyledons

questions.q_en: Which of the following organelles is responsible for photosynthesis in plants?
questions.solution_en:
• Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which is crucial for photosynthesis. Other options:

• Mitochondria: Involved in respiration and energy production.

• Nucleus: Contains genetic material.

• Lysosome: Involved in waste breakdown and recycling of cellular material.

Further Insight:

• Plant Cell:

• Type: Eukaryotic cell, found in plants.

• Cell Wall: Present; made of cellulose, providing structural strength.

• Key Organelles:

○ Nucleus: Contains genetic material (DNA).

○ Mitochondria: Produces energy (ATP).

○ Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER): Involved in protein and lipid synthesis.

○ Golgi Apparatus: Packaging and transportation of proteins.

○ Chloroplasts: Enable photosynthesis (conversion of light energy into chemical energy).

○ Large Central Vacuole: Maintains turgor pressure and stores nutrients.

• Other Features: Contains plasmodesmata (channels for communication between cells).

questions.q_en: What is the primary source of energy for autotrophic plants?
questions.solution_en:
• Autotrophic plants use sunlight to produce food through photosynthesis. Other options:

• Nitrogen: Required for plant growth but not an energy source.

• Water: Used in photosynthesis but is not the primary energy source.

• Oxygen: Produced as a byproduct of photosynthesis, not an energy source.

questions.q_en: Which process is unique to sexual reproduction in angiosperms?
questions.solution_en:
• Double fertilization occurs in angiosperms, where one sperm fertilizes the egg, and the other forms the endosperm. Other processes:

• Binary fission: Occurs in unicellular organisms, the mother cell divided into two daughter cells.

• Spore formation: Common in lower plants like bryophytes and fungi.

Further Insight:

• Double fertilization is a unique feature of angiosperms, involving two fusion events in the ovule. After pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma, forming a pollen tube that carries two male gametes to the ovule.

• First Fertilization (Syngamy): One sperm cell fuses with the egg cell, forming a diploid zygote (2n), which later develops into the embryo.

• Second Fertilization (Triple Fusion): The other sperm cell fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell, forming a triploid (3n) endosperm. This endosperm nourishes the developing embryo.

• Significance:

○ Zygote Formation: The zygote develops into the embryo.

○ Endosperm Formation: The triploid endosperm serves as a food source for the embryo and helps in seed germination.

•

■ Rhodophyceae (Red Algae): Marine, chlorophyll a & d, e.g., Polysiphonia, Gelidium.

questions.q_en: Which of the following algae is widely used for agar-agar production?
questions.solution_en:
Gelidium is a red algae (Rhodophyceae) used for the production of agar-agar, a gelatinous substance used in food and microbiology. Other options:

• (1) Spirogyra: A type of green algae, not used for agar.

• (3) Chlamydomonas: A unicellular green algae with no commercial use for agar.

• (4) Fucus: A brown algae, used for other purposes like fertilizer

Further Insight:

• Algae have several economic uses across various sectors:

• Food Source: Algae, particularly marine forms like Laminaria, Sargassum, and Porphyra, are consumed as food in many Asian countries. They are rich in proteins, vitamins, and minerals.

• Agar-Agar Production: Algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria are used to extract agar, which is extensively used in microbiology for culturing microorganisms and as a stabilizer in food and cosmetics.

• Biofertilizers: Algae like Azolla and Anabaena fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching soil fertility. These algae are used as biofertilizers, especially in paddy fields.

• Commercial Products: Alginates from brown algae (e.g., Laminaria) and carrageenan from red algae (e.g., Chondrus) are used in the food, textile, and pharmaceutical industries as thickeners, stabilizers, and emulsifiers.

• Aquaculture Feed: Algae serve as a feedstock for fish and other marine organisms in aquaculture.

• Potential Biofuel Source: Algae are being explored as a renewable source of biofuels due to their high lipid content and fast growth rate.

questions.q_en: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Mosses?
options_en: The sporophyte is independent of the gametophyte
questions.solution_en:
• In mosses (a type of bryophyte), the gametophyte is the dominant stage of the life cycle. Other options:

• Vascular tissues: Absent in bryophytes

• Sporophyte independent: The sporophyte in bryophytes is dependent on the gametophyte.

• True roots: Mosses have rhizoids, not true roots

Further Insight:

• Bryophytes are non-vascular land plants that thrive in moist environments.

• They lack true roots, stems, and leaves but possess structures analogous to them, like rhizoids for anchorage.

• Bryophytes reproduce through spores and play an essential role in preventing soil erosion and maintaining moisture in ecosystems.

• They are often called "amphibians of the plant kingdom" as they require water for reproduction.

• Classes of Bryophytes:

○ Hepaticopsida (Liverworts):

■ These plants have flat, liver-shaped thalli.

■ Reproduce asexually via gemmae cups.

■ Examples: Marchantia, Riccia.

○ Anthocerotopsida (Hornworts):

■ Have a flattened thallus and long horn-like sporophytes.

■ Sporophytes continuously grow from their base.

■ Examples: Anthoceros, Notothylas.

○ Bryopsida (Mosses):

■ Possess small, leaf-like structures around a central stem.

■ Mosses undergo a life cycle with a dominant gametophyte and a sporophyte attached to it.

■ Examples: Funaria, Sphagnum.

questions.q_en: Which of the following pteridophyte classes has homosporous plants?
questions.solution_en:
• Psilopsida (primitive pteridophytes) are homosporous, meaning they produce spores of the same size.

• Lycopsida: Can be heterosporous or homosporous.

• Sphenopsida: Mostly homosporous.

• Pteropsida: Mostly heterosporous.

Further Insight:

• Pteridophytes are vascular plants with true roots, stems, and leaves but reproduce via spores instead of seeds. They are considered the first land plants with vascular tissues (xylem and phloem), enabling better water and nutrient transport.

○ Classes of Pteridophytes:

■ Psilopsida (Whisk ferns):

• Simple, rootless plants with rhizomes.

• Example: Psilotum.

■ Lycopsida (Club mosses):

• Small, evergreen plants with true roots and leaves.

• Example: Lycopodium.

■ Sphenopsida (Horsetails):

• Hollow, jointed stems with scale-like leaves.

• Example: Equisetum.

■ Pteropsida (Ferns):

• Large fronds with a complex vascular system.

• Example: Pteris.

○ Pteridophytes can be divided into two groups based on the types of spores they produce:

■ Homosporous Pteridophytes:

• Produce only one type of spore that develops into a bisexual gametophyte.

• Example: Pteris.

■ Heterosporous Pteridophytes:

• Produce two types of spores:

○ Microspores (male gametophyte)

○ Megaspores (female gametophyte)

• Example: Selaginella, Salvinia.

questions.q_en: Which of the following plants is an example of gymnosperm?
questions.solution_en:

Further Insight:

• Features:

○ Woody, perennial, and may form large trees.

○ Taproot system, with leaves that may be simple or compound.

○ Reproduce through heterospory (microspores and megaspores).

questions.q_en: Gymnosperms differ from angiosperms in which of the following ways?
questions.solution_en:
• Gymnosperms do not have flowers. Their seeds are produced on cones and are exposed.

• Both gymnosperms and angiosperms have xylem and phloem.

• Gymnosperms have naked seeds, not enclosed in fruits.

• Both groups have chlorophyll for photosynthesis.

questions.q_en:
Consider the following statements regarding Pteridophytes:

(a) Pteridophytes possess true roots, stems, and leaves.

(b) Pteridophytes produce seeds for reproduction.

(c) The dominant phase in their life cycle is the sporophyte.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution_en:
• Pteridophytes have well-differentiated roots, stems, and leaves, unlike bryophytes.

• Pteridophytes reproduce through spores, not seeds.

• The dominant phase in the life cycle of pteridophytes is the sporophyte (diploid), while the gametophyte is reduced.

Further Insight:

• Pteridophytes are vascular plants with true roots, stems, and leaves but reproduce via spores instead of seeds. They are considered the first land plants with vascular tissues (xylem and phloem), enabling better water and nutrient transport.

○ Classes of Pteridophytes:

■ Psilopsida (Whisk ferns):

• Simple, rootless plants with rhizomes.

• Example: Psilotum.

■ Lycopsida (Club mosses):

• Small, evergreen plants with true roots and leaves.

• Example: Lycopodium.

■ Sphenopsida (Horsetails):

• Hollow, jointed stems with scale-like leaves.

• Example: Equisetum.

■ Pteropsida (Ferns):

• Large fronds with a complex vascular system.

• Example: Pteris.

questions.q_en:
Consider the following statements about Gymnosperms:

(a) Gymnosperms produce seeds that are enclosed within fruits.

(b) They lack xylem vessels in their vascular tissues.

(c) Gymnosperms are generally woody, with no herbaceous species.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution_en:
• Gymnosperms produce naked seeds, not enclosed within fruits (unlike angiosperms).

• Gymnosperms lack xylem vessels; they have tracheids instead for water conduction.

• Gymnosperms are typically woody plants, and they do not have herbaceous representatives.

Further Insight:

Gymnosperms

• Non-flowering, seed-bearing plants with seeds that are exposed (not enclosed in fruits).

• Examples: Pinus, Cycas, Cedrus.

• Features:

○ Woody, perennial, and may form large trees.

○ Taproot system, with leaves that may be simple or compound.

○ Reproduce through heterospory (microspores and megaspores).

○ Gymnosperms lack xylem vessels; they have tracheids instead for water conduction

questions.q_en:
Consider the following statements regarding the features of Monocot Seeds:

(a) Monocot seeds possess a single cotyledon.

(b) Monocot seeds exhibit hypogeal germination.

(c) In monocot seeds, the endosperm is usually absent.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution_en:
• Monocot seeds have one cotyledon, which is a key feature distinguishing them from dicots.

• Many monocot seeds show hypogeal germination, where the cotyledon remains underground.

• In monocot seeds, the endosperm is generally present and provides nourishment to the growing seedling.

Further Insight:
